p.src:
Mathematically, $\ket{\psi}$ and $e^{i\chi}\ket{\psi}$ are different vectors. Physically, they represent the same pure state. Let $\ket{\psi'}=e^{i\chi}\ket{\psi}.$ The corresponding bra is $\bra{\psi'}=e^{-i\chi}\bra{\psi}.$ Every expectation value is unchanged: $\begin{aligned}
  \bra{\psi'}\hat K\ket{\psi'}
  &=
  e^{-i\chi}\bra{\psi}\hat K
  e^{i\chi}\ket{\psi}\\
  &=
  \bra{\psi}\hat K\ket{\psi}.
  \end{aligned}$ The phase is an ordinary scalar and commutes through $\hat K$.

An equivalent parameterization makes the geometry especially transparent: $\ket{\psi}

p.src:
The ellipse needs two independent real parameters. One gives the orientation of its major axis. The other gives its shape together with the sense of rotation. The lecture informally calls the latter a signed eccentricity. In standard optics it is cleaner to use the signed ellipticity angle $\epsilon$: $-\frac{\pi}{4}\leq\epsilon\leq\frac{\pi}{4},
  \qquad
  \left|\tan\epsilon\right|
  =\frac{\text{minor semiaxis}}{\text{major semiaxis}}.$ The sign records handedness. Linear polarization has $\epsilon=0$; circular polarization has $|\epsilon|=\pi/4$, where the major-axis direction becomes meaningless.

p.src:
The transmission probability is $\begin{aligned}
  P_\theta
  &=
  |\braket{\theta}{\psi}|^2\\
  &=
  a^2\cos^2\theta
  +b^2\sin^2\theta
  +2ab\cos\phi\,\sin\theta\cos\theta\\
  &=
  \frac12
  \left[
    1
    +(a^2-b^2)\cos2\theta
    +2ab\cos\phi\,\sin2\theta
  \right].
  \end{aligned}$ The lecture leaves this multiplication and maximization as homework. Finishing that step makes its geometric prescription exact. The major-axis angle $\theta_{\mathrm{maj}}$ obeys $2\theta_{\mathrm{maj}}
  =
  \operatorname{atan2}
  \left(2ab\cos\phi,\ a^2-b^2\right)
  \pmod{2\pi}.$ Thus the analyzer most likely to transmit the photon points along the major axis of the polarization ellipse.

p.src: For a closed reversible classical system, evolution is one-to-one. It may permute the states, but it cannot send two distinct initial states to the same final state. If both $5$ and $2$ on a die evolved to $3$, the final state would not reveal which initial state had been prepared. The distinction would have been erased.

p.src:
Prepare two identical systems in $\ket{A}$ and $\ket{B}$, and let both evolve for the same time: $\ket{A}\longrightarrow\ket{A'},
  \qquad
  \ket{B}\longrightarrow\ket{B'}.$ Closed-system quantum evolution preserves their inner product: $\boxed{\braket{B'}{A'}=\braket{B}{A}.}$ Consequently equal rays remain equal rays, orthogonal states remain orthogonal, and every transition probability remains unchanged. This is the quantum form of preserving distinctions.

p.src:
The expectation value of a Hermitian operator is real: $\begin{aligned}
  \left(
    \bra{\psi}\hat L\ket{\psi}
  \right)^*
  &=
  \bra{\psi}\hat L^\dagger\ket{\psi}\\
  &=
  \bra{\psi}\hat L\ket{\psi}.\end{aligned}$ Conversely, in finite dimensions, if $\bra{\psi}\hat L\ket{\psi}$ is real for every $\ket{\psi}$, then $\hat L$ is Hermitian.

p.src: Unitary Operators Preserve Quantum Relations

u.src: Unitary Operators Preserve Quantum Relations
en: Unitary Operators Preserve Quantum Relations

p.src:
Hermitian operators represent quantities that can be measured. They are not, in general, the transformations that move states while preserving their relations. Let one linear operator $\hat U$ act on every state: $\hat U\ket{A}=\ket{A'},
  \qquad
  \hat U\ket{B}=\ket{B'}.$ The transformed bras are $\bra{A'}=\bra{A}\hat U^\dagger,
  \qquad
  \bra{B'}=\bra{B}\hat U^\dagger.$ Therefore $\braket{B'}{A'}
  =
  \bra{B}\hat U^\dagger\hat U\ket{A}.$ Demanding equality with $\braket{B}{A}$ for every pair $\ket{A},\ket{B}$ forces $\boxed{\hat U^\dagger\hat U=\mathbf 1.}$

p.src:
In finite dimensions this condition makes $\hat U$ invertible and implies $\hat U^\dagger=\hat U^{-1},
  \qquad
  \hat U\hat U^\dagger
  =\hat U^\dagger\hat U
  =\mathbf 1.$ In an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, the definition of a unitary operator includes both equalities; $\hat U^\dagger\hat U=\mathbf1$ alone defines an isometry that need not be onto.

p.src:
The lecture closes just as the eigenvalue structure of a unitary operator is introduced: $\hat U\ket{n}=\lambda_n\ket{n}.$ The unanswered question has a short consequence of unitarity: $\begin{aligned}
  1
  &=
  \braket{n}{n}
  =
  \bra{n}\hat U^\dagger\hat U\ket{n}\\
  &=
  |\lambda_n|^2\braket{n}{n},\end{aligned}$ so $|\lambda_n|=1,
  \qquad
  \lambda_n=e^{i\omega_n}.$ Finite-dimensional unitary matrices are normal and therefore possess a complete orthonormal eigenbasis, but their eigenvalues are phases rather than necessarily real numbers.
